structure.title: Part I · Rehearsing an act
structure.text: Raskolnikov counts steps, inspects a room and listens to chance remarks as if the city were sending him instructions. A letter from his mother and an encounter in a tavern put urgent claims on his sympathy while he is trying to turn a killing into an intellectual proposition.

structure.title: Parts II–III · The body gives evidence
structure.text: The crime leaves him with doors to answer, clothes to examine and appointments he cannot face. Friends arrive with soup and practical suggestions. In his fever, even the most ordinary kindness can feel like an attempt to discover what happened.

structure.title: Parts IV–VI and epilogue · Different listeners
structure.text: An investigator has read something Raskolnikov published. Sonya knows what it costs to be judged by strangers. What he can tell each of them differs, and so does what each might do with the truth. The epilogue asks how far an official account of a crime can reach into a life.

people.name: Raskolnikov
people.text: He can give a stranger his last coins and resent the same stranger's need an instant later. His argument about exceptional men promises an escape from humiliating dependence. The experiment depends on knowing in advance what sort of man he is.

people.name: Sonya Marmeladova
people.text: Sonya's father tells her story to men in a tavern before we meet her. Raskolnikov comes to her with a story about her too. Her quiet disagreements matter precisely because so many men assume they already understand her sacrifice.

people.name: Porfiry Petrovich
people.text: He invites a suspect to discuss ideas at the very moment a straightforward question would be easier to answer. His jokes have a peculiar afterlife. Raskolnikov can leave the room and continue interrogating himself on Porfiry's behalf.

context.title: A theory about permission
context.text: Raskolnikov imagines that people who bring a new order into the world may have to break the old order's laws. Napoleon is an attractive example for someone living alone above a staircase. The much harder case is the woman standing a few feet away.

notice.text: Look at the rooms available for a private conversation.
notice.why: Thin partitions, lodgers, open doors and crowded stairs give even a whispered exchange a possible audience. The struggle to conceal a deed begins in a city where it is difficult simply to be alone.

notice.text: Keep track of money as it changes hands.
notice.why: A gift can be an apology, an insult, an attempt to purchase authority or an immediate answer to hunger. Raskolnikov's explanations often arrive after his hand has already moved.

opening: Raskolnikov has an argument for murder. The woman he intends to kill is a predatory pawnbroker; her money could finance a useful life, and great men have done worse for less. He wants to know whether he belongs among those who can step over the law. Dostoevsky follows him from the argument into the deed and its aftermath, where an ordinary conversation can become unbearable and the need to conceal what he has done begins competing with the need for someone to know.
